original_value: Real-time identification of the occurrence of dangerous pathogens is of crucial importance for the rapid execution of countermeasures. For this purpose, spatial and temporal predictions of the spread of such pathogens are indispensable. The R package papros developed by the authors offers an environment in which both spatial and temporal predictions can be made, based on local data using various deterministic, geostatistical regionalisation, and machine learning methods. The approach is presented using the example of a crops infection by fungal pathogens, which can substantially reduce the yield if not treated in good time. The situation is made more difficult by the fact that it is particularly difficult to predict the behaviour of wind-dispersed pathogens, such as powdery mildew (Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici). To forecast pathogen development and spatial dispersal, a modelling process scheme was developed using the aforementioned R package, which combines regionalisation and machine learning techniques. It enables the prediction of the probability of yield- relevant infestation events for an entire federal state in northern Germany at a daily time scale. To run the models, weather and climate information are required, as is knowledge of the pathogen biology. Once fitted to the pathogen, only weather and climate information are necessary to predict such events, with an overall accuracy of 68% in the case of powdery mildew at a regional scale. Thereby, 91% of the observed powdery mildew events are predicted.

result.paraphrase: Rapid identification of dangerous pathogens is essential for swiftly implementing countermeasures, and this requires spatial and temporal forecasts of their spread. To support this, the authors’ R package papros provides a framework for making both spatial and temporal predictions from local data using deterministic, geostatistical regionalisation, and machine learning methods. The method is illustrated with crop infection caused by fungal pathogens, which can markedly reduce yield if left untreated. Predicting the behavior of wind-dispersed pathogens, such as powdery mildew (Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici), is especially challenging. A modelling workflow was therefore developed with the R package to forecast pathogen development and dispersal, combining regionalisation and machine learning techniques. It allows daily prediction of the probability of yield-relevant infestation events for an entire federal state in northern Germany. Model run requires weather and climate information plus knowledge of pathogen biology; after fitting to the pathogen, only weather and climate data are needed. For powdery mildew at regional scale, the overall accuracy is 68%, and 91% of observed powdery mildew events are predicted.
